title: The younger son (Luke 15:11–24)
hookLine: he came to himself, rehearsed a speech, and his father interrupted it with a hug
carry: while he was still far off

lines: A CERTAIN MAN HAD TWO SONS.
cards: Have you ever rehearsed an apology? In the car, in the shower, at three in the morning. You polish every line and lower your expectations so you won't be disappointed.
Today's story has a young man doing exactly that, on a long walk home. People call it the prodigal son, though Luke never gives it a title. Jesus just begins: a certain man had two sons.

teach.b: The younger son asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father is alive. Some commentators say that in that world it was close to saying I wish you were dead. The father divides it anyway.
The son goes to a far country and wastes it all. Then famine.

He ends up feeding pigs, animals his own people's law counted unclean, and in the King James Bible, "he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him."
As low as he can go.

teach.h: HE RAN, WHILE THE SON WAS FAR OFF.
teach.b: He works out a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants." Not a son again, just a paid worker.

Then the line that turns the story: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Some readers think he'd been watching the road.
And he ran; some commentators note that grown men of standing didn't run in public.

The son starts the speech, and before he gets to make me a hired servant, the father interrupts, calling to the servants: "Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet."
Robe, ring and shoes: you don't put those on a worker. You put them on a son.

teach.h: THIS MY SON WAS DEAD, AND IS ALIVE AGAIN.
teach.b: And the father says why: "this my son was dead, and is alive again."

how: Christians read this story often, especially in Lent; Catholics and Orthodox Christians often connect it with confession, and many churches use it to welcome people who are returning after years away.

o: the inner organs, where compassion is felt
the best robe, given to an honored son

Luke calls this story the parable of the prodigal son

the father saw his son while he was still a great way off
"his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran."

games.q: you're the father. far down the road you see a thin figure walking slowly toward the house. it's your son. what do you do?
o: wait at the door to hear what he has to say.
run to him, and hold him before he says a word.
send a servant to find out what he wants.
games.why: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."

practice: Think of somewhere you've drifted from, a person, a promise, a practice, a faith, and notice the speech you've been rehearsing for going back: the explanations, the bargaining, the lowered expectations.
Then picture the father on the road, already running before you've said a word, and let the speech go quiet.
If you pray, simply turn toward God without the speech; if you don't, let yourself be welcomed, in your imagination, before you've earned it.

wordCard.voice: Splanchna, the Greek word for the inner organs, where compassion is felt — what moved the father to run to his younger son, met on the road before he could finish his speech.

orig.note: Greek: he had compassion, felt it in his gut. from splanchna, the inner organs.

carryVoice: Your line: while he was still far off. The father ran first. Day five hundred fifty-eight, done.
